trial_name: Leuven 1 — Intensive Insulin Therapy vs Conventional Glucose Control in Surgical ICU (2001)
citation: Van den Berghe G, Wouters P, Weekers F, Verwaest C, Bruyninckx F, Schetz M, et al. Intensive insulin therapy in critically ill patients. N Engl J Med. 2001;345(19):1359-67
one_liner: In a single-centre surgical ICU, intensive insulin therapy targeting 80–110 mg/dL reduced ICU mortality (4.6% vs 8.0%) and major morbidities, but subsequent multicentre trials did not reproduce the benefit and practice shifted to moderate glycaemic targets.

pico.population: Adult mechanically ventilated patients admitted to a surgical ICU (February 2000–January 2001)
pico.intervention: Continuous IV insulin infusion started if glucose >110 mg/dL, titrated to maintain 80–110 mg/dL (maximum 50 IU/h)
pico.comparison: Continuous IV insulin infusion started only if glucose >215 mg/dL, titrated to maintain 180–200 mg/dL
pico.outcome: Primary: ICU mortality (death during ICU stay); secondary: in‑hospital mortality, bloodstream infections, renal replacement therapy, prolonged ventilation (>14 days), critical‑illness polyneuropathy, hypoglycaemia

background.existing_knowledge: Stress hyperglycaemia and insulin resistance are common in critical illness, even in non‑diabetic patients. Observational data link hyperglycaemia to infections, organ failure, neuromuscular complications, and death.
background.knowledge_gap: No controlled trial evidence existed in ICU patients. Surgical ICUs deliver high early glucose/caloric loads (often parenterally), potentially amplifying hyperglycaemia.
background.hypothesis: Normalising blood glucose with intensive insulin therapy would reduce severe infections, polyneuropathy, organ failure, and death.

methods.design: Prospective, randomised, controlled, single‑centre, open‑label, parallel‑group superiority trial.
methods.setting: Surgical ICU, Leuven, Belgium; February 2, 2000 – January 18, 2001.

inclusion: All adults receiving mechanical ventilation admitted to the ICU during enrolment
Written informed consent from closest family member

methods.intervention: Continuous IV insulin infusion started if glucose >110 mg/dL, titrated to 80–110 mg/dL (4.4–6.1 mmol/L); max 50 IU/h. Whole‑blood arterial glucose checked every 1–4 h, nurse‑driven protocol with study physician oversight. Standardised nutrition: IV glucose 200–300 g/24 h day 1, then scheduled parenteral/enteral feeding (20–30 non‑protein kcal/kg/day, 0.13–0.26 g N/kg/day, 20–40% lipids).
methods.comparison: Continuous IV insulin only if glucose >215 mg/dL, titrated to 180–200 mg/dL (10.0–11.1 mmol/L). Same glucose monitoring framework and identical standardised nutrition.
methods.blinding: Unblinded (insulin titration requires frequent glucose results). Insulin team separate from clinical decisions; key outcome analyses blinded.
methods.sample_size_power: Planned enrolment 2500 to detect 5% absolute mortality difference in >5‑day stay patients; stopped early after 1548 at fourth interim analysis due to superiority of intensive arm. Power not explicitly reported.
secondary_outcomes: Critical‑illness polyneuropathy (EMG in surviving screened subgroup)
methods.follow_up: Through ICU stay and hospital stay (survivors considered alive at discharge). Survival curves extended to ~250 days for in‑hospital mortality.

headline_bullets: ICU mortality: 4.6% vs 8.0% (adjusted risk reduction 32%, 95% CI 2–55, P<0.04 after sequential adjustment).
In‑hospital mortality: 7.2% vs 10.9% (unadjusted P=0.01); mortality benefit concentrated in patients staying >5 ICU days: 10.6% vs 20.2% (P=0.005).

Major morbidity reductions: bloodstream infection 4.2% vs 7.8% (relative reduction 46%, P=0.003), renal replacement therapy 4.8% vs 8.3% (41% reduction, P=0.007), prolonged ventilation >14 days 7.5% vs 11.9% (P=0.003), polyneuropathy in screened survivors 28.7% vs 51.4% (P<0.001).
Hypoglycaemia ≤40 mg/dL: 39 (5.1%) vs 6 (0.8%) patients; two symptomatic events, no haemodynamic compromise.
Among ICU stay >5 days: median ICU LOS 12 vs 15 days (P=0.003), cumulative TISS‑28 431 vs 563 (P<0.001), and polyneuropathy screening differential (20.5% vs 26.3% screened).

outcomes_table.note: Apparent RR 0.58; Lan‑DeMets sequential adjustment applied.
Unadjusted; sequential correction not applied to non‑primary endpoints.

outcomes_table.outcome: Death during ICU, ICU stay >5 days
outcomes_table.note: Early ICU deaths (≤5 days) similar: 13/557 vs 14/540.
Peak creatinine and urea nitrogen lower in intensive arm (medians reported).
Median ventilation days in >5‑day stay: 10 vs 12 (P=0.006).
Screening rates: 20.5% intensive vs 26.3% conventional (fewer screened because ICU stays were shorter).
Two symptomatic events in intensive group (sweating, agitation); no haemodynamic deterioration or convulsions.

subgroup_table.note: Benefit reported as consistent across cardiac and non‑cardiac surgery subgroups; no formal interaction P‑value provided.

safety: Two symptomatic events (sweating, agitation) in intensive group; no haemodynamic deterioration or convulsions.
No other serious adverse events reported.

domains.notes: Sealed envelopes, permuted blocks of 20, stratified by diagnostic category, balanced for sex/diabetes. Only 14 pre‑randomisation exclusions (very limited selection filtering).
Unblinded (frequent glucose measurement). Insulin titration separated from clinical decisions via a nurse‑led protocol and study physician, with blinded analysis of key outcomes.
ITT for mortality outcomes; no post‑randomisation exclusions reported. Some morbidity endpoints (e.g., EMG screening) conditionally assessed on survival/duration.
High insulin delivery in intensive arm (98.7% received insulin) vs 39.2% in conventional; median daily insulin dose 71 vs 33 IU/day; 100% vs 67% of ICU stay receiving insulin.
Groups similar in demographics, diabetes prevalence (13%), and admission hyperglycaemia. APACHE II may be artificially lowered for post‑resuscitation/sedated patients.

internal_validity.verdict: Moderate: randomisation, objective mortality, and ITT analysis support causal inference, but single‑centre, unblinded design and early stopping limit confidence in effect size and multiplicity of secondary endpoints.

domains.notes: Predominantly surgical (64% cardiac surgery), mechanically ventilated adults. Admission hyperglycaemia common but marked hyperglycaemia (>200 mg/dL) in only 12%.

Protocol required 1–4 hourly arterial glucose measurements, nurse‑driven titration, and early high IV glucose nutrition (200–300 g/24 h). Not easily replicated in medical ICUs or resource‑limited settings.

external_validity.verdict: Limited generalisability to non‑surgical ICU populations and settings without similar monitoring infrastructure and nutritional protocols.

strengths: Large randomised trial for its era in ICU metabolic management.
Marked separation of glycaemic exposure: morning glucose 103±19 vs 153±33 mg/dL; insulin use 98.7% vs 39.2%.
Clinically meaningful endpoints: ICU and in‑hospital mortality, sepsis, RRT, ventilation, and electrophysiologically‑defined polyneuropathy.
Pre‑specified interim monitoring with Lan‑DeMets sequential adjustment for the primary endpoint.
limitations: Single‑centre design in a predominantly post‑operative surgical ICU.
Unblinded delivery (inherent to frequent glucose monitoring).
Early stopping after fourth interim analysis may inflate effect size estimates.
Nominal (unadjusted) P‑values for morbidity endpoints; multiple secondary outcomes without correction.
Polyneuropathy screening subset with differential screening proportions (20.5% vs 26.3%).
Substantial increase in hypoglycaemia (39 vs 6 patients), a critical safety concern.

critical_appraisal.summary: An early, well‑separated comparison with striking morbidity and mortality signals, but irreproducible in subsequent multicentre trials; high risk of bias from unblinding and early stopping limits confidence in the magnitude of effect.
strengths: Rigorous randomisation with minimal pre‑enrolment exclusions
Large observed biochemical separation between arms
weaknesses: Stopped early with sequential adjustment only on primary outcome
Multiplicity of morbidity endpoints without adjustment
Hypoglycaemia imbalance confounds net clinical benefit

sections.authors_conclusion: Intensive insulin therapy to maintain blood glucose at or below 110 mg/dL reduces ICU and in‑hospital mortality and morbidity among critically ill surgical patients.

clinical_bottom_line.verdict: This trial does not change modern practice; subsequent multicentre evidence (notably NICE‑SUGAR) found increased mortality and hypoglycaemia with tight targets. Current guidelines recommend initiating insulin when glucose exceeds 180 mg/dL and targeting 140–180 mg/dL while avoiding strict normoglycaemia.
clinical_bottom_line.applies_to: Historical interest only; the benefits observed in this well‑resourced surgical cohort were not replicated in broader ICU populations.
clinical_bottom_line.does_not_mean: All ICU patients should be managed with tight (80–110 mg/dL) glucose targets.
implementation_caveats: Tight glycaemic targets substantially increase hypoglycaemia risk and require intensive monitoring and dedicated nursing protocols.
The nutritional regimen (early high IV glucose load) differs from modern ICU feeding strategies, which may influence outcomes.

controversies.topic: Early stopping and effect size inflation
controversies.notes: The trial was terminated at 12 months after the fourth interim analysis, a design that can overestimate treatment effects. The adjusted risk reduction (32%) is smaller than the apparent observed reduction (42%).

A subsequent Leuven trial in a medical ICU (Leuven 2) did not show uniform mortality benefit. NICE‑SUGAR subsequently demonstrated worse survival with tight control in a mixed medical‑surgical population.
Hypoglycaemia (≤40 mg/dL) was 5.1% vs 0.8%; two symptomatic episodes. VISEP and GLUCONTROL in sepsis/mixed ICUs reinforced the hazard of hypoglycaemia without survival advantage.

Pooled analyses of ICU glycaemic trials found no consistent mortality benefit with tight targets and increased hypoglycaemia. Contemporary guidelines (e.g., SCCM, ADA) recommend initiating insulin at glucose ≥180 mg/dL and targeting a moderate range (140–180 mg/dL).

context_related_trials.relation: Same investigators; did not reproduce the same uniform mortality benefit in a medical ICU population.

Large multicentre RCT (n=6104) comparing tight (81–108 mg/dL) vs conventional (≤180 mg/dL) control; found increased mortality (27.5% vs 24.9%) and severe hypoglycaemia with tight control—directly contradicting Leuven 1.
Multicentre RCT in severe sepsis; no mortality benefit and high rates of hypoglycaemia led to early discontinuation of tight control arm.
Multicentre RCT in mixed ICU; did not demonstrate a clear mortality benefit and highlighted feasibility/safety concerns.

unresolved_questions: Optimal glucose target in various ICU subpopulations (surgical vs medical vs sepsis).
Interaction between nutritional strategy (especially parenteral glycaemic load) and glycaemic targets.
Whether a subset of patients (e.g., cardiac surgery) still benefits from tighter control.

numbers_to_remember: Major morbidity: sepsis 4.2% vs 7.8% (46% reduction), dialysis 4.8% vs 8.3% (41% reduction)
quick_recall.one_line_takeaway: Leuven 1 showed that intensive insulin therapy to 80–110 mg/dL reduced ICU death in a surgical cohort, but subsequent multicentre trials failed to replicate the benefit and tight glucose targets are no longer recommended for general ICU care.
